meta.title: The Depot at the Center of Town
meta.intro: It is the 1890s. You are Ada Pruitt, 16, whose family farms cotton outside Woodstock. Make up to five choices and see how the railroad shaped the town you know today. About 5 minutes.
meta.characterNote: Ada Pruitt and her family are fictional composite characters. Places, dates and events marked “True history” come from the cited sources.

route.name: Dave Haney Home
route.blurb: Built circa 1908 and home to David J. and Edna McCleskey Haney for many years. Later occupants included Canton newspaper editor Joe Parham; J.E., S.L. and S.L. Johnston Jr. bought it, and in 1946 sold it to J.D. and Edison Whitmire, whose family lived here until 1979. The two-story house keeps much of its wrap-around porch with pilasters and Victorian-style woodwork.

quiz.q: Which family lived here from 1946 until 1979?

photo.alt: Photo of Dave Haney Home, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 1, 8256 Main St.

route.name: Linton Dean Home
route.blurb: Originally built circa 1918 for Claude Chandler, then bought by Linton Dean in 1931 for $3,000. He lived here with his wife Alice Wellons Dean and daughters Elizabeth and Alice. It is a craftsman bungalow with tapered square columns and a porte-cochère, and a badminton court on the back lawn drew young people to the home.

quiz.q: What did Linton Dean pay for the house in 1931?

photo.alt: Photo of Linton Dean Home, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 2, 8262 Main St.

route.name: Latimer-Howell Home
route.blurb: Built in 1906 for Wylie P. Dobbs and soon sold to Thomas E. Latimer for $100. His sister Martha Latimer owned it from 1907 to 1937. In 1943 L. E. Howell bought the house, and it stayed in the Howell family until 2001. Its Victorian style was enhanced when it was renovated for commercial use; the wide veranda once wrapped around two sides.

quiz.q: How long did the Howell family keep the house?

photo.alt: Photo of Latimer-Howell Home, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 3, 8358 Main St.

route.name: Woodstock School
route.blurb: The older section—two wings joined by a gymnasium/auditorium—survived the 1939 fire that destroyed the original schoolhouse. The addition built after the fire has a bell cupola still in evidence, and other facilities came in the 1960s. The school relocated in 2005, and Chattahoochee Technical College occupies the campus today.

quiz.q: What happened to the original schoolhouse in 1939?

photo.alt: Photo of Woodstock School, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 4, 8371 Main St.

route.name: Emmett Dial Home
route.blurb: Built for Emmett Dial about 1910 and first occupied by Mr. Dial, his sister and brother-in-law. Later he married Mary Claude Simpson, and they lived here until their deaths; their only child, Sara Frances, was born in the home. Mr. Dial was Woodstock's postmaster from 1917 to 1933. Look for the front porch that curves gracefully to one side and the clipped gable roofline.

quiz.q: What job did Emmett Dial hold from 1917 to 1933?

photo.alt: Photo of Emmett Dial Home, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 5, 8425 Main St.

route.name: W.D. Bozeman Home
route.blurb: Built circa 1910 by L. J. Runyon and first occupied by the W. D. Bozeman family; three of the four Bozeman daughters kept living here, and the last passed away in 2003. The white prairie-style house has four square 4-over-4 double-hung sash windows, a corner tower, a bay window and a vintage staircase 27 inches wide.

quiz.q: How wide is the vintage staircase?

photo.alt: Photo of W.D. Bozeman Home, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 6, 109 Rope Mill Rd.

route.name: Woodstock Presbyterian Church
route.blurb: The original Bethesda Presbyterian Church north of Woodstock burned in 1916. In 1923 it relocated, was renamed Woodstock Presbyterian Church, and this building went up; the congregation used it until 1989. The decorative woodwork under the gables is unique to the town, and in fall a yellow maple lights up the steeple.

quiz.q: What was the church called before it moved in 1923?

photo.alt: Photo of Woodstock Presbyterian Church, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 7, 101 Rope Mill Rd.

route.name: W.L. Dean Home
route.blurb: Built circa 1875; Dr. William Lemuel and Lou Boring Dean lived here beginning in 1883, and their seven children were born here. The architecture recalls an English cottage. The bricks were made in the yard, the front porch columns came from the Canton hotel, and ivy planted over the front bay window in 1885 thrived for years.

quiz.q: Where did the front porch columns come from?

photo.alt: Photo of W.L. Dean Home, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 8, 103 East Main St.

route.name: J.H. Johnston Home
route.blurb: Built in 1913 after the original wood house burned along with nearby Woodstock Baptist Church. Mr. Johnston was a local merchant and founder of the Bank of Woodstock. He married Avis Benson and they had ten children; their son Joseph E. Johnston lived here until his death in 1978. Note the six Ionic columns on the front porch.

quiz.q: How many Ionic columns are on the front porch?

photo.alt: Photo of J.H. Johnston Home, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 9, 8516 Main St.

route.name: Woodstock Baptist Church
route.blurb: Originally Enon Baptist Church, north of town; the congregation moved into town in 1879. In 1884 it was renamed Woodstock Baptist Church and a new meeting house was built. That burned in 1913 and was replaced by this sanctuary, with a flat bell tower, no steeple, and arched stained-glass windows that once swiveled open. The bricks match the Johnston House next door. The congregation moved in 1991.

quiz.q: Why do this church's bricks match the house next door?
options: Same builder's bricks as the Johnston House

photo.alt: Photo of Woodstock Baptist Church, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 10, 8534 Main St.

route.name: Post Office
route.blurb: Woodstock had postmasters as early as 1833, with mail handled in homes or businesses. This building, constructed circa 1908, was the first used only as a post office. John T. Morgan, postmaster 1909–1915, was also a builder. A faux stone facade covers the original brick storefront. In 1961 the post office moved to 8604/8606 Main St., and W. H. Howard later ran Woodstock Jewelry here.

quiz.q: Before this building, where was Woodstock's mail handled?

photo.alt: Photo of Post Office, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 11, 8558 Main St.

route.name: Cotton Warehouse
route.blurb: The J. H. Johnston cotton warehouse, circa 1905, is the last of several such warehouses in Woodstock. Cotton was stored on the upper floor, which opened onto Church Street; crews moved 500-pound bales from wagons, and each bale was weighed and tagged with a receipt for weight, date and quality. The basement was too humid for cotton, so fertilizer and plows were kept there.

quiz.q: Why was cotton kept upstairs instead of in the basement?

photo.alt: Photo of Cotton Warehouse, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 12, 105 Towne Lake Pkwy. (formerly Church St.)

route.name: Woodstock Methodist Church
route.blurb: Home to the oldest church in continuous operation in the same building in the city. Built in 1889, with major improvements in 1924 including brick walls. A 1953 redesign added Sunday School rooms, a basement, a kitchen and restrooms. Stained-glass windows and stately trees add to its charm.

quiz.q: When was this church building constructed?

photo.alt: Photo of Woodstock Methodist Church, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 13, 109 Towne Lake Pkwy.

route.name: Bank of Woodstock
route.blurb: Before 1908 this was the site of a livery stable. J. H. Johnston built the current structure in 1908 for the Bank of Woodstock, which stayed until 1972 when it moved to 8770 Main St. From 1972 to 1989 the building housed the Woodstock Public Library. Note the golden brick and decorative brickwork; 1970s photos showed a hitching post on the Church Street side.

quiz.q: What stood on this site before 1908?

photo.alt: Photo of Bank of Woodstock, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 14, 8578 Main St.

route.name: Dobbs-Chandler Building
route.blurb: Built by Amanda Chandler Edwards circa 1905. The first business here was a grocery and general merchandise store run by Claude Chandler. Later came Hendon Grocery, Williams Food Store, Dawson-Parr Department Store, and Keenum's Gift and Toyland.

quiz.q: What kind of store came first?
options: A grocery and general merchandise store

photo.alt: Photo of Dobbs-Chandler Building, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 15, 8582 Main St.

route.name: Dean's Store
route.blurb: This building and 8582 Main St. were presumably built at the same time, with matching facades, roof lines and a common wall; it dates to circa 1905 or earlier. Owner Dr. W. H. Dean was one of the town's original settlers. His son Dr. Will Dean opened Dean's Drug Store here in 1906 with his son Linton Dean, who ran it until his death in 1981. Today the intact store is home to the Woodstock Visitors Center.

quiz.q: What is in Dean's Store today?

photo.alt: Photo of Dean's Store, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 16, 8588 Main St.

route.name: Woodstock Depot
route.blurb: Built in 1912 to replace the first depot, which was later demolished. It has tongue-and-groove siding and a red clay tile roof—typical North Georgia railroad depot architecture with Victorian-era influence—and served as a combination station for freight and passengers. The depot and tracks were the center of the city's original boundaries in the 1897 charter. It is the only structure in Woodstock on the National Register of Historic Places.

quiz.q: What was measured from the depot in the 1897 charter?

photo.alt: Photo of Woodstock Depot, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 17, 251 E Main St.

route.name: Original Location of J.H. Johnston Company
route.blurb: Believed to be the first location of the J. H. Johnston Company, General Mercantile and Cotton Brokers, established in 1888 and the major business in Woodstock for eight decades. The Woodstock Masonic Lodge used the second floor until recent years, along with the telephone exchange. The Bank of Woodstock began here before moving to its new building in 1908.

quiz.q: Which bank started inside this store?

photo.alt: Photo of Original Location of J.H. Johnston Company, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 18, 8590/8594 Main St.

route.name: Chandler Building
route.blurb: Mack Dobbs is believed to have been the first owner, circa 1913. He ran a funeral parlor here with partner Claude Chandler, and a mule-drawn hearse was kept on the premises. Ernest Thompson later reportedly had a used Ford parts business, and in the 1970s Riley Medley ran a family restaurant. The cast iron Meskers on either side of the double front doors, with a fleur-de-lis design, are unique in Woodstock.

quiz.q: What pulled the funeral parlor's hearse?

photo.alt: Photo of Chandler Building, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 19, 8636 Main St.

route.name: Jail
route.blurb: Originally a brick building where L. J. Runyon carved monuments circa 1914. It was a cannery during World War II and became city property in 1952. The fire truck was parked here and it was known as Old City Hall; later occupants used "Olde Towne Hall" as a business name. Bars on a single window recall the days it held prisoners before transfer to the county jail.

quiz.q: What was this building used for during World War II?

photo.alt: Photo of Jail, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 20, 8654 Main St. (rear)

route.name: Johnston-Neese Home
route.blurb: Traces its origin to J. H. Johnston circa 1890. His son Walt Johnston lived here, then retired Methodist minister John Wesley Gober. The Smith L. Johnston Jr. family moved in in the late 1940s. Doc Neese bought it in 1954 and it stayed with the Neese family until 1985, when the William Johnston family became owners. Look for Queen Anne elements and a street-level porch with decorative woodwork.

quiz.q: Who bought the house in 1954?

photo.alt: Photo of Johnston-Neese Home, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 21, 8864 Main St.

route.name: S.L. Johnston Home
route.blurb: Soon after their marriage in 1917, Smith Lemon Johnston and Florine Dial moved into this new brick craftsman-style bungalow, designed by a friend and built for $1,700. Their four children grew up here; after Mrs. Johnston's death it became the home of the youngest son, William J. Johnston. Its structure has been carefully maintained.

quiz.q: What did the bungalow cost to build?

photo.alt: Photo of S.L. Johnston Home, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 22, 8870 Main St.

route.name: Sam Dawson Home
route.blurb: Built in 1909 by Sam and Georgia Carpenter Dawson, originally surrounded by porches on all sides. Sliding pocket doors led from the reception hall to the parlor, and the dining room sat in the center of the house with no windows. Original fireplaces and mantels remain, and the basic design can still be seen.

quiz.q: What was unusual about the dining room?

photo.alt: Photo of Sam Dawson Home, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 23, 8990 Main St.

route.name: W.D. Power Home
route.blurb: Built in 1912 for Walter Dean Power and his bride Nellie Dobbs: a white frame house with a brick foundation, twelve-foot ceilings, a colonnade between living and dining rooms, and a wide pine staircase to the bedrooms. Each of the three Power children was born in the ground-floor bedroom. The yard had a garage, a stable for a horse and cow, and later a tennis court. The Power family lived here for ninety years.

quiz.q: How long did the Power family live here?

photo.alt: Photo of W.D. Power Home, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 24, 9021 Main St.

route.name: Olde Rope Mill Park
route.address: Rope Mill Rd., about 1 mile north of downtown
route.maps: Olde Rope Mill Park, Woodstock, GA
route.blurb: Since the 1840s and maybe earlier, grist mills worked this stretch of Little River. The 1880 census lists the Joel T. Haley mill making cotton yarns using the river's slight drop for power. The final cotton mill, Rope Mill (1928–1949), made rope for wells, plow lines and tents; Joe Johnston and Smith Johnston Sr. were the last owners. It closed in 1949 after the U.S. Government bought the land for Allatoona Lake. Ruins and signs are in the park today.

quiz.q: What did Rope Mill make from 1928 to 1949?
options: Rope for wells, plow lines and tents

photo.alt: Photo of Olde Rope Mill Park, Downtown Woodstock walking tour stop 25, a bridge over the river, Rope Mill Rd.

s1.title: Harvest at the Tracks
text: Your father's wagon creaks toward the depot with bales of cotton. Before the trains came, families here mostly grew what they needed. Now the rails run straight through the village.
Father hands you the reins. “You decide where we take this load first.”
s1.fact: The Marietta & North Georgia Railroad reached Woodstock in 1879 on its line from Marietta to Canton. A first depot stood on the west side of the tracks, and farmers used the line to ship cotton to mills. (Today's depot at this stop replaced that first depot in 1912.)

choices.label: Go to the depot and ship the cotton by rail
Stop at the big general store on Main Street

s2a.title: The Depot Agent
text: The depot agent tallies your bales, and the telegraph clicks behind him. Trains carry mail, goods and passengers to Marietta and beyond.
A man on the platform says the town may soon become an official city.
s2a.fact: The depot was the focal point for shipping cotton, rope and farm products, and for travelers heading to Canton and Marietta. It had an agent and telegraph service.

choices.label: Ask the man what becoming a city would mean

s2b.title: Johnston's Store
text: Main Street is lined with businesses on its west side, and cotton warehouses stand across the way. At the J.H. Johnston Company you can sell your cotton and buy supplies in the same trip.
The clerk mentions talk of a town charter.
s2b.fact: This is believed to be the first location of the J.H. Johnston Company, General Mercantile and Cotton Brokers, established in 1888. The Woodstock Masonic Lodge and the telephone exchange used the second floor, and the Bank of Woodstock began in the store before moving to its own building in 1908.

choices.label: Ask the clerk about the charter

s3.title: A Town Measured from the Depot
text: News arrives: the Georgia legislature has granted Woodstock a charter. Folks gather to hear how the new town lines were drawn.
Everyone laughs when they hear where the measuring started.
s3.fact: On December 8, 1897, the Georgia legislature chartered Woodstock. City limits ran ¾ mile north and south of the depot and ½ mile east and west of the tracks, making the depot the center of town. Nathan Fowler was the first mayor. The 1900 census counted 276 residents.
s3.prompt: Years pass. Where does your future lead?

choices.label: Stay in town and help with the family's cotton business
Look for work at the mill on Little River

s_wh.title: Weighing Day at the Warehouse
text: You drive the wagon up to the Johnston cotton warehouse on Church Street. A work crew wrestles each heavy bale off the wagon and onto the scale.
The clerk hands you a receipt. Down on Main Street, Dr. W.H. Dean's store is open for business. Your father asks what to do with the money.
s_wh.fact: The J.H. Johnston cotton warehouse, built around 1905, is the last of several such warehouses in Woodstock. Crews moved 500-pound bales by hand into the upper floor, which opened onto Church Street. Each bale was weighed and tagged, and the owner got a receipt showing weight, date and quality. The humid basement held fertilizer, plows and other farm equipment instead. Dean's Store at 8588 Main St. was built around 1905 or earlier; Dr. W.H. Dean was the owner, and the building is now the Woodstock Visitors Center.

choices.label: Save it and watch the town grow around the depot
Buy a new plow from the warehouse basement

s4.title: A New Depot
text: You are grown now. Crews finish a new wooden depot beside the tracks, with a red clay tile roof, a freight room and a passenger waiting area.
Your niece asks whether to ride the train to school in Canton or Marietta.
s4.fact: The Louisville & Nashville Railroad bought the line in 1905 and built the current depot in 1912 on the east side of the tracks, replacing the first depot, which was later torn down. It has tongue-and-groove siding and a red clay tile roof, typical North Georgia depot design with Victorian touches, and served as a “combination station” for freight and passengers. Like other L&N depots of the time, it had a separate entrance and waiting room for Black passengers under segregation.

choices.label: Tell her to take the train to school
Tell her to stay and build something in Woodstock

s4m.title: The Mill on Little River
text: North of town, Little River drops just enough to turn a mill wheel, and the mill spins local cotton. The work is loud and long, but the pay is steady.
A foreman asks if you will train the new hands.
s4m.fact: Grist mills worked this stretch of Little River from the 1840s or earlier. The 1880 census shows the Joel T. Haley mill making cotton yarns, using the river's slight drop to power textile machinery. A series of owners and cotton businesses followed.

choices.label: Return to town and the depot

c1_a.title: The Wrap-Around Porch
text: You are Ada Pruitt, now a young woman, delivering a basket of eggs along Main Street. The new two-story house at 8256 Main St. has a porch that wraps around the front, trimmed with Victorian-style woodwork.

choices.label: Admire the porch trim from the street
Wonder who will live here over the years

c1_b0.title: Pilasters and Woodwork
text: You count the pilasters holding up the porch roof and trace the carved trim with your eyes. Houses in town are getting fancier.

choices.label: Sketch the trim in your notebook
Walk on before your eggs get warm

c1_b1.title: Many Families
text: A house like this will see many families. You imagine the porch full of different voices across the decades.

choices.label: Picture the porch fifty years from now

c2_a.title: The Badminton Court
text: You are Clara Pruitt, Ada's niece, a teenager in the 1930s. Word around town is that the craftsman bungalow at 8262 Main St. has a badminton court on the back lawn, and young people gather there.

choices.label: Bring a friend and walk by on a Saturday

c2_b0.title: Saturday on the Lawn
text: From the sidewalk you can see the porte-cochère, the covered drive at the side, and hear the shuttlecock being hit back and forth.

choices.label: Practice your swing on the way home

c2_b1.title: Tapered Columns
text: You notice the square porch columns get narrower toward the top, a craftsman-bungalow look that is popular now.

choices.label: Remember it for your own house someday

c3_a.title: A House for $100
text: You are Ada Pruitt, a teenager. Folks are talking about a house at 8358 Main St.: built this year, and already sold for just $100.
c3_a.prompt: What do you make of it?

choices.label: Ask your father whether $100 is a lot

c3_b0.title: Counting the Cost
text: Father says $100 is real money to a cotton family, but a bargain for a whole house. You make a note to remember the price.

choices.label: Wonder who will own it next

c3_b1.title: The Veranda
text: The wide veranda wraps around two sides of the house, shading it from the summer sun.

choices.label: Imagine sitting out on a hot evening

c4_a.title: Fire at the Schoolhouse
text: You are Clara Pruitt, a young teacher in 1939. The original schoolhouse at 8371 Main St. has burned. The newer wings, joined by a gymnasium and auditorium, survived.

choices.label: Help gather books from the surviving wings

c4_b0.title: Saving What Survived
text: You and other townsfolk carry books and slates into the gymnasium. Classes will go on.

choices.label: Set up a classroom in the auditorium
Make a list of what was lost

c4_b1.title: A Bell Cupola
text: Plans are drawn for an addition with a bell cupola on top. You imagine the bell calling children for years to come.

c5_a.title: The Postmaster's House
text: You are Ada Pruitt, picking up mail. The postmaster in these years, Emmett Dial, lives in the house at 8425 Main St., built about 1910.

c5_b0.title: A Graceful Curve
text: The front porch curves gracefully around one side. You have not seen another like it in town.

choices.label: Run your hand along the rail as you pass

c5_b1.title: The Clipped Gable
text: The ends of the roof are clipped off at an angle, a clipped gable, which sets this house apart.

choices.label: Point it out to a friend

c6_a.title: The Corner Tower
text: You are Ada Pruitt on Rope Mill Road. A new white house at 109 Rope Mill Rd., built about 1910 by L. J. Runyon, has a corner tower and a bay window.

c6_b0.title: Four-over-Four
text: Each tall window has four panes over four, double-hung sashes that slide up and down.

choices.label: Count them again to be sure

c6_b1.title: A Narrow Stair
text: You hear the house has a staircase only 27 inches wide. You picture carrying a trunk up it and laugh.

c7_a.title: A Church Moves to Town
text: You are Clara Pruitt. The old Bethesda Presbyterian Church north of town burned in 1916. Now, in 1923, the congregation has relocated and renamed itself Woodstock Presbyterian Church, at 101 Rope Mill Rd.

c7_b0.title: Unique Woodwork
text: Decorative woodwork decorates the gables, unlike any other building in town.

c7_b1.title: A Yellow Maple
text: There are two maples by the church. In fall, the yellow one lights up the steeple.

choices.label: Come back in October to see it

c8_a.title: Bricks from the Yard
text: You are Ada Pruitt's grandmother as a young woman in the 1880s. A house at 103 East Main St., built about 1875, looks like an English cottage, and its bricks were made right in the yard.

choices.label: Ask how bricks are made in a yard

c8_b0.title: Clay and Fire
text: Clay is dug, shaped and fired nearby. You marvel that a house can rise from its own ground.

c8_b1.title: Columns from Canton
text: You learn the front porch columns came from the Canton hotel. Ivy has been planted over the front bay window.

choices.label: Watch the ivy grow over the years

c9_a.title: Six Ionic Columns
text: You are Ada Pruitt. A fire took the old wooden house at 8516 Main St. along with nearby Woodstock Baptist Church. Now a new house rises, built in 1913, for J. H. Johnston, a local merchant and founder of the Bank of Woodstock.

c9_b0.title: Six Columns
text: Six tall Ionic columns, with scrolled tops, line the front porch.

c9_b1.title: Rebuilding
text: The town rebuilds after the fire. You see new brick going up next door at the church too.

c10_a.title: The Bell Tower Without a Steeple
text: You are Ada Pruitt. The Baptist meeting house burned in 1913, and a new brick sanctuary is going up at 8534 Main St. with a flat bell tower and no steeple.

c10_b0.title: Windows That Swivel
text: Arched stained-glass windows swivel open from the center to let in summer air.

c10_b1.title: Matching Bricks
text: The bricks match the Johnston House next door.

c11_a.title: The First Post Office Building
text: You are Ada Pruitt. For years Woodstock's mail was handled in homes and businesses. Now there's a building at 8558 Main St., built about 1908, used only as a post office.

choices.label: Mail a letter to a cousin in Marietta

c11_b0.title: A Letter by Rail
text: You hand over your letter. It will likely ride the train from the depot.

choices.label: Ask how long it will take

c11_b1.title: Brick Storefront
text: The building has a brick storefront. Years later it will be hidden behind a faux stone face.

c12_a.title: Weighing Day
text: You are Ada Pruitt. You drive the wagon up to the J. H. Johnston cotton warehouse on Church Street. A work crew lifts each 500-pound bale onto the scale.

c12_b0.title: The Receipt
text: The bale is weighed and tagged, and you get a receipt showing the weight, date and quality.

choices.label: Fold the receipt into your pocket
Ask what the price is today

c12_b1.title: Fertilizer and Plows
text: The basement is too humid for cotton, so fertilizer and plows are stored there.

c13_a.title: The Oldest Church Building
text: You are Clara Pruitt. The Methodist church at 109 Towne Lake Pkwy., built in 1889, is getting major improvements this year, including brick walls.

c13_b0.title: New Walls
text: Bricks go up around the old building. It will still be the same church building, just stronger.

c13_b1.title: Growing Church
text: You picture Sunday School rooms, a kitchen and a basement someday. They will be added in 1953.

c14_a.title: From Livery to Bank
text: You are Ada Pruitt. At 8578 Main St. a livery stable used to rent out horses. In 1908 a golden-brick building rises there for the Bank of Woodstock.

choices.label: Open a savings account with your cotton money

c14_b0.title: Your First Account
text: The bank's decorative brickwork shines. You leave with a little book showing your deposit.

choices.label: Tie your horse at the hitching post

c14_b1.title: Bank to Library
text: Decades later, from 1972 to 1989, the building will become the Woodstock Public Library.

c15_a.title: Groceries on Main Street
text: You are Ada Pruitt with your mother's list. The building at 8582 Main St., built about 1905, holds a grocery and general merchandise store.

c15_b0.title: Shopping Day
text: You get flour and coffee, and you watch other families stocking up for the week.

c15_b1.title: A Store of Many Lives
text: Over the years this storefront will become other groceries, a department store and even a toy store, Keenum's Gift and Toyland.

c16_a.title: Dean's Drug Store
text: You are Ada Pruitt. Dr. Will Dean has opened Dean's Drug Store in the building at 8588 Main St., which shares a wall and matching front with its neighbor.

choices.label: Pick up a remedy for your mother

c16_b0.title: At the Counter
text: You wait at the counter while your order is filled. The store will run for decades.

c16_b1.title: Twin Storefronts
text: 8582 and 8588 Main St. have matching facades and rooflines, as if built together.

c17_a.title: The New Depot
text: You are Ada Pruitt. A new depot is going up at 251 E Main St. to replace the first one, with tongue-and-groove siding and a red clay tile roof.

c17_b0.title: Combination Station
text: It is a combination station, serving both freight and passengers.

c17_b1.title: Center of Town
text: You remember the 1897 charter measured the town limits from the depot. The depot really is the center of town.

c18_a.title: Johnston's Store
text: You are Ada Pruitt as a girl. The J. H. Johnston Company at 8590/8594 Main St., established in 1888, sells general goods and buys cotton.

c18_b0.title: Two Errands at Once
text: You sell the cotton and buy cloth and nails in one trip.

c18_b1.title: The Second Floor
text: The Masonic Lodge and the telephone exchange are upstairs. The Bank of Woodstock started here too.

c19_a.title: The Fleur-de-Lis Doors
text: You are Ada Pruitt. The brick building at 8636 Main St., built about 1913, houses a funeral parlor, and a mule-drawn hearse is kept on the premises.

choices.label: The mule in the stable yard

c19_b0.title: Meskers
text: Cast iron panels called Meskers frame the double doors, with a fleur-de-lis design found nowhere else in town.

c19_b1.title: The Hearse Mule
text: The patient mule waits, ready for solemn days.

c20_a.title: Old City Hall
text: You are Clara Pruitt, now a grown woman. The small brick building behind 8654 Main St. was a monument carver's shop about 1914 and a cannery in World War II. In 1952 the city took it over.

c20_b0.title: Fire Truck Inside
text: The town fire truck is parked here, and folks call it Old City Hall.

c20_b1.title: Holding Cell
text: One window has bars. The city holds prisoners here before taking them to the county jail.

c21_a.title: Queen Anne Porch
text: You are Ada Pruitt. A house at 8864 Main St. begun about 1890 has Queen Anne touches and a street-level porch with decorative woodwork.

choices.label: Wonder how long it will last

c21_b0.title: Decorative Woodwork
text: The porch trim is carved and curved, ready to be painted.

c21_b1.title: A Long Life
text: The house will pass through several families, and the Neese family will own it from 1954 to 1985.

c22_a.title: A $1,700 Bungalow
text: You are Ada Pruitt. A new brick craftsman bungalow at 8870 Main St. was designed by a friend of the newlyweds who own it and built for $1,700.

choices.label: Compare it to the $100 house you saw years ago

c22_b0.title: Prices Change
text: $1,700! Things have changed since the $100 house of 1906.

c22_b1.title: A Family Home
text: You picture a family of four children growing up behind the brick walls.

c23_a.title: Porches All Around
text: You are Ada Pruitt. The new house at 8990 Main St., built in 1909, has porches on all sides.

c23_b0.title: Sliding Pocket Doors
text: The doors from the reception hall to the parlor slide into the walls.

c23_b1.title: A Room in the Middle
text: The dining room sits in the middle of the house, with rooms all around and no windows.

c24_a.title: Twelve-Foot Ceilings
text: You are Ada Pruitt. A white frame house on a brick foundation is finished at 9021 Main St. in 1912, with twelve-foot ceilings and a wide pine staircase.

c24_b0.title: Between the Rooms
text: A row of columns stands between the living and dining rooms.

c24_b1.title: Stable and Garden
text: The large yard has a garage and a stable for a horse and cow. Later there'll be a tennis court.

c25_a.title: Rope Mill on Little River
text: You are Clara Pruitt. North of town on Little River, the Rope Mill (1928–1949) makes rope for wells, plow lines and tents.

c25_b0.title: Twisting Rope
text: Machines twist cotton into strong rope. The river's small drop powers it all.

c25_b1.title: An Old Site
text: Mills have worked here since the 1840s or earlier. Someday the U.S. Government will buy the land for Allatoona Lake, and the mill will close.

e_rails.title: Ending: The Line to the Wider World
text: Your niece rides the train to school each day, part of a generation the rails connected to wider Georgia.
history: Students rode the train from the Woodstock depot to school in Canton and Marietta. Passenger service ended on March 1, 1949, and the depot kept freight and telegraph service until the late 1950s.

e_town.title: Ending: The Center Still Holds
text: Your family stays and helps the little town grow around its depot.
history: The 1912 depot still stands and is on the National Register of Historic Places, the only such listing in Woodstock. Main Street was paved in 1912. Woodstock grew from about 4,500 to about 36,000 residents over three decades.

e_mill.title: Ending: Cotton into Rope
text: You become one of the experienced hands at the mill, teaching others the trade as owners come and go.
history: The last cotton mill on the site, Rope Mill (1928–1949), made rope for wells, plow lines and tents. Joe Johnston and Smith Johnston Sr. were its last owners. It closed in 1949 after the U.S. Government bought the property for Lake Allatoona. Ruins of the mill and history signs are in Olde Rope Mill Park today.

c1_end.title: Memory saved: a sketch of a wrap-around porch
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a sketch of a wrap-around porch.
history: Built circa 1908 and home to David J. and Edna McCleskey Haney for many years. Later occupants included Canton newspaper editor Joe Parham; J.E., S.L. and S.L. Johnston Jr. bought it, and in 1946 sold it to J.D. and Edison Whitmire, whose family lived here until 1979. The two-story house keeps much of its wrap-around porch with pilasters and Victorian-style woodwork.

c2_end.title: Memory saved: a badminton shuttlecock
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a badminton shuttlecock.
history: Originally built circa 1918 for Claude Chandler, then bought by Linton Dean in 1931 for $3,000. He lived here with his wife Alice Wellons Dean and daughters Elizabeth and Alice. It is a craftsman bungalow with tapered square columns and a porte-cochère, and a badminton court on the back lawn drew young people to the home.

c3_end.title: Memory saved: a slip of paper reading “$100”
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a slip of paper reading “$100”.
history: Built in 1906 for Wylie P. Dobbs and soon sold to Thomas E. Latimer for $100. His sister Martha Latimer owned it from 1907 to 1937. In 1943 L. E. Howell bought the house, and it stayed in the Howell family until 2001. Its Victorian style was enhanced when it was renovated for commercial use; the wide veranda once wrapped around two sides.

c4_end.title: Memory saved: a schoolhouse bell
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a schoolhouse bell.
history: The older section—two wings joined by a gymnasium/auditorium—survived the 1939 fire that destroyed the original schoolhouse. The addition built after the fire has a bell cupola still in evidence, and other facilities came in the 1960s. The school relocated in 2005, and Chattahoochee Technical College occupies the campus today.

c5_end.title: Memory saved: a postage stamp
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a postage stamp.
history: Built for Emmett Dial about 1910 and first occupied by Mr. Dial, his sister and brother-in-law. Later he married Mary Claude Simpson, and they lived here until their deaths; their only child, Sara Frances, was born in the home. Mr. Dial was Woodstock's postmaster from 1917 to 1933. Look for the front porch that curves gracefully to one side and the clipped gable roofline.

c6_end.title: Memory saved: a pane of window glass
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a pane of window glass.
history: Built circa 1910 by L. J. Runyon and first occupied by the W. D. Bozeman family; three of the four Bozeman daughters kept living here, and the last passed away in 2003. The white prairie-style house has four square 4-over-4 double-hung sash windows, a corner tower, a bay window and a vintage staircase 27 inches wide.

c7_end.title: Memory saved: a yellow maple leaf
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a yellow maple leaf.
history: The original Bethesda Presbyterian Church north of Woodstock burned in 1916. In 1923 it relocated, was renamed Woodstock Presbyterian Church, and this building went up; the congregation used it until 1989. The decorative woodwork under the gables is unique to the town, and in fall a yellow maple lights up the steeple.

c8_end.title: Memory saved: a handmade brick
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a handmade brick.
history: Built circa 1875; Dr. William Lemuel and Lou Boring Dean lived here beginning in 1883, and their seven children were born here. The architecture recalls an English cottage. The bricks were made in the yard, the front porch columns came from the Canton hotel, and ivy planted over the front bay window in 1885 thrived for years.

c9_end.title: Memory saved: a scroll from an Ionic column
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a scroll from an Ionic column.
history: Built in 1913 after the original wood house burned along with nearby Woodstock Baptist Church. Mr. Johnston was a local merchant and founder of the Bank of Woodstock. He married Avis Benson and they had ten children; their son Joseph E. Johnston lived here until his death in 1978. Note the six Ionic columns on the front porch.

c10_end.title: Memory saved: a chip of stained glass
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a chip of stained glass.
history: Originally Enon Baptist Church, north of town; the congregation moved into town in 1879. In 1884 it was renamed Woodstock Baptist Church and a new meeting house was built. That burned in 1913 and was replaced by this sanctuary, with a flat bell tower, no steeple, and arched stained-glass windows that once swiveled open. The bricks match the Johnston House next door. The congregation moved in 1991.

c11_end.title: Memory saved: a letter stamped “Woodstock, Ga.”
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a letter stamped “Woodstock, Ga.”.
history: Woodstock had postmasters as early as 1833, with mail handled in homes or businesses. This building, constructed circa 1908, was the first used only as a post office. John T. Morgan, postmaster 1909–1915, was also a builder. A faux stone facade covers the original brick storefront. In 1961 the post office moved to 8604/8606 Main St., and W. H. Howard later ran Woodstock Jewelry here.

c12_end.title: Memory saved: a cotton receipt
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a cotton receipt.
history: The J. H. Johnston cotton warehouse, circa 1905, is the last of several such warehouses in Woodstock. Cotton was stored on the upper floor, which opened onto Church Street; crews moved 500-pound bales from wagons, and each bale was weighed and tagged with a receipt for weight, date and quality. The basement was too humid for cotton, so fertilizer and plows were kept there.

c13_end.title: Memory saved: a Sunday School card
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a Sunday School card.
history: Home to the oldest church in continuous operation in the same building in the city. Built in 1889, with major improvements in 1924 including brick walls. A 1953 redesign added Sunday School rooms, a basement, a kitchen and restrooms. Stained-glass windows and stately trees add to its charm.

c14_end.title: Memory saved: a bank deposit book
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a bank deposit book.
history: Before 1908 this was the site of a livery stable. J. H. Johnston built the current structure in 1908 for the Bank of Woodstock, which stayed until 1972 when it moved to 8770 Main St. From 1972 to 1989 the building housed the Woodstock Public Library. Note the golden brick and decorative brickwork; 1970s photos showed a hitching post on the Church Street side.

c15_end.title: Memory saved: a grocery list
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a grocery list.
history: Built by Amanda Chandler Edwards circa 1905. The first business here was a grocery and general merchandise store run by Claude Chandler. Later came Hendon Grocery, Williams Food Store, Dawson-Parr Department Store, and Keenum's Gift and Toyland.

c16_end.title: Memory saved: a medicine bottle label
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a medicine bottle label.
history: This building and 8582 Main St. were presumably built at the same time, with matching facades, roof lines and a common wall; it dates to circa 1905 or earlier. Owner Dr. W. H. Dean was one of the town's original settlers. His son Dr. Will Dean opened Dean's Drug Store here in 1906 with his son Linton Dean, who ran it until his death in 1981. Today the intact store is home to the Woodstock Visitors Center.

c17_end.title: Memory saved: a train ticket
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a train ticket.
history: Built in 1912 to replace the first depot, which was later demolished. It has tongue-and-groove siding and a red clay tile roof—typical North Georgia railroad depot architecture with Victorian-era influence—and served as a combination station for freight and passengers. The depot and tracks were the center of the city's original boundaries in the 1897 charter. It is the only structure in Woodstock on the National Register of Historic Places.

c18_end.title: Memory saved: a store token
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a store token.
history: Believed to be the first location of the J. H. Johnston Company, General Mercantile and Cotton Brokers, established in 1888 and the major business in Woodstock for eight decades. The Woodstock Masonic Lodge used the second floor until recent years, along with the telephone exchange. The Bank of Woodstock began here before moving to its new building in 1908.

c19_end.title: Memory saved: a fleur-de-lis drawing
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a fleur-de-lis drawing.
history: Mack Dobbs is believed to have been the first owner, circa 1913. He ran a funeral parlor here with partner Claude Chandler, and a mule-drawn hearse was kept on the premises. Ernest Thompson later reportedly had a used Ford parts business, and in the 1970s Riley Medley ran a family restaurant. The cast iron Meskers on either side of the double front doors, with a fleur-de-lis design, are unique in Woodstock.

c20_end.title: Memory saved: a fire truck bell
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a fire truck bell.
history: Originally a brick building where L. J. Runyon carved monuments circa 1914. It was a cannery during World War II and became city property in 1952. The fire truck was parked here and it was known as Old City Hall; later occupants used "Olde Towne Hall" as a business name. Bars on a single window recall the days it held prisoners before transfer to the county jail.

c21_end.title: Memory saved: a curl of porch trim
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a curl of porch trim.
history: Traces its origin to J. H. Johnston circa 1890. His son Walt Johnston lived here, then retired Methodist minister John Wesley Gober. The Smith L. Johnston Jr. family moved in in the late 1940s. Doc Neese bought it in 1954 and it stayed with the Neese family until 1985, when the William Johnston family became owners. Look for Queen Anne elements and a street-level porch with decorative woodwork.

c22_end.title: Memory saved: a builder's estimate
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a builder's estimate.
history: Soon after their marriage in 1917, Smith Lemon Johnston and Florine Dial moved into this new brick craftsman-style bungalow, designed by a friend and built for $1,700. Their four children grew up here; after Mrs. Johnston's death it became the home of the youngest son, William J. Johnston. Its structure has been carefully maintained.

c23_end.title: Memory saved: a fireplace tile
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a fireplace tile.
history: Built in 1909 by Sam and Georgia Carpenter Dawson, originally surrounded by porches on all sides. Sliding pocket doors led from the reception hall to the parlor, and the dining room sat in the center of the house with no windows. Original fireplaces and mantels remain, and the basic design can still be seen.

c24_end.title: Memory saved: a pine shaving from the staircase
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a pine shaving from the staircase.
history: Built in 1912 for Walter Dean Power and his bride Nellie Dobbs: a white frame house with a brick foundation, twelve-foot ceilings, a colonnade between living and dining rooms, and a wide pine staircase to the bedrooms. Each of the three Power children was born in the ground-floor bedroom. The yard had a garage, a stable for a horse and cow, and later a tennis court. The Power family lived here for ninety years.

c25_end.title: Memory saved: a piece of rope
text: You add a new memory to the book you carry along the tour: a piece of rope.
history: Since the 1840s and maybe earlier, grist mills worked this stretch of Little River. The 1880 census lists the Joel T. Haley mill making cotton yarns using the river's slight drop for power. The final cotton mill, Rope Mill (1928–1949), made rope for wells, plow lines and tents; Joe Johnston and Smith Johnston Sr. were the last owners. It closed in 1949 after the U.S. Government bought the land for Allatoona Lake. Ruins and signs are in the park today.

finale.title: The Memory Book Is Full
text: You have walked all 25 stops of Historic Downtown Woodstock and saved a memory at each one, from a cotton receipt to a piece of rope from the mill on Little River.
The characters were fictional, but every building and date you met is real. Most of them are still standing, a short walk from the depot at the center of town.
